newsitem.title: RUSSIA: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN ARMY AT WAR WITH PROMOTED ALTER EGO.
newsitem.headline: ICE HOCKEY-RUSSIAN ARMY AT WAR WITH PROMOTED ALTER EGO.

text.p: CSKA Moscow, the Russian army club, are celebrating promotion to ice hockey's top division after last week's victory in the junior league playoffs.
But lawyers for CSKA Moscow said on Monday they would fight the advance all the way through the courts.

The conundrum has its roots in the split in the ranks of the Central Army Sporting Club (CSKA) which led to the creation of two rival hockey squads and which nearly saw the CSKA Moscow soccer club barred from this season's premiership.

Viktor Tikhonov, who coached the Soviet Union to world hockey dominance in the 1980s, fell out with his army employers and, after a long court battle, won the right last year for his privately-backed team to use the CSKA name and facilities.
That left Colonel Alexander Baranovsky and his army club playing under the same name in a lower division -- a situation which was, if not entirely satisfactory, at least workable.
But that all changed when the other CSKA, coached by Alexander Volkhov, won promotion.
A spokesman for the Army Sports Club said the promoted side aimed to strip Tikhonov of the name and right to use Moscow's CSKA arena through two separate court cases.
Yuri Zemlyakov told Reuters: "Tikhonov was sacked as CSKA coach in 1993 and has no relationship to the Army Sports Club. All they are doing is renting our rink and other facilities."
But Inna Gushchina, lawyer for Tikhonov's CSKA, said she was confident of winning the case at an April 21 court hearing.
A similar dispute last winter between rival CSKA's in soccer forced the football league to order the two claimants to settle or see neither of them taking part in this season's competition.
The army, which has been fighting against severe funding shortages since the collapse of the Soviet Union, won out over a businessman and sacked CSKA soccer coach Alexander Tarkhanov.

The Russian Ice Hockey Federation has not made up its mind what to do. Vice-president Yuri Kovalyov told Reuters the federation wanted to give the rivals time to reach a settlement. He personally thought they should simply merge the two teams.
"But if they can't find a common language," Kovalyov said, "Why not call them CSKA I and CSKA II?"
